claims.text: The magnetocaloric response of as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloys is governed by strain-induced stabilization of nanostructured interfacial regions.
Strained grain-boundary regions pin the magnetostructural transition and govern its hysteresis.
Controlled thermal annealing relieves internal stresses.
Controlled thermal annealing reduces the density of strained interfacial regions.
Reducing internal stress and strained interfacial-region density will decrease magnetocaloric hysteresis.
Reducing internal stress and strained interfacial-region density will smooth the entropy-change response under low-field cycling.
The as-deposited material has a highly textured, ordered single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited material contains residual stress and a high density of grain boundaries or interfacial defects.
Grain boundaries and interfacial defects act as nucleation or pinning sites for the magnetostructural transition.
Residual stress and high grain-boundary density promote a sharp, strongly hysteretic magnetostructural transition.
Annealing lowers pinning and the energy barriers for phase transformation by relaxing or reducing interfacial features.
Lower pinning and transformation barriers decrease hysteresis and broaden the magnetocaloric transition.
Annealed samples will exhibit a broader and smoother magnetocaloric entropy-change profile than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed samples will exhibit less hysteresis than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed samples will retain a substantial overall entropy change.
As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi films display a sharp first-order magnetostructural transition with a large but highly hysteretic magnetocaloric effect.
The prediction applies only while annealing relieves strain without causing unwanted grain growth, phase separation, or loss of single-phase hexagonal ordering.
High-surface-to-volume-ratio sample geometry enables rapid heat exchange.
Failure to reduce hysteresis or broaden the transition despite confirmed reduction of grain-boundary density or strain would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes a stabilized interfacial 'phase,' whereas the initial state and boundary describe the alloy as single-phase hexagonal. It is unclear whether 'interfacial phase' means a distinct crystallographic phase, which would conflict with the single-phase description, or merely strained interfacial material.
